Class 10B group, 9:14 pm
Nirmala: who got 38 in maths 👀
Rehan: not me 😅
Nirmala: Tenzin bro your mom's gonna frame that paper
Rehan: 😆
Tenzin is typing…
Tenzin: at least I don't copy from the topper like some people
Tenzin: and it was 41 btw
Nirmala: ok chill it was a joke
Tenzin: your jokes are trash, like your handwriting
Rehan: ooooh
Tenzin stared at the screen. His thumbs had moved before his head did. The 41 was on his desk under his geometry box, and he had been avoiding it all evening, afraid it proved what he secretly thought: that he just wasn't good enough for science. If he stayed quiet now, everyone would decide the joke was true.

passage: Kishan was pumping a tyre at his father's cycle shop in Sirsa when the phone on the counter buzzed three times. The tuition batch group. Jyoti had posted a photo of the notice board with the unit test marks, a circle around his name: 52. "Kishan bhai, see you in Class 11 again next year? 😄" Rehana added a laughing face. Something cold dropped in his stomach. His father always said the shop was waiting if studies didn't work out, and lately Kishan had started to wonder whether that was a joke or a plan. He wiped his greasy thumb on his shirt and typed fast: "Say that after your English result, Jyoti. Two tuitions and still 40?" He hit send before he could read it again.

The hostel common room was loud with the TV, but Yash only heard his phone buzz.
The Class 11 group chat: Binita had posted, "Yash got 38 in physics again, someone give him a medal 🏅" Four laughing reactions came in within seconds.
His stomach dropped. He had studied for that test until one at night. Maybe he really was the dumb one in the batch. Maybe everyone already knew it.
He didn't wait to think. His thumbs were already moving: "At least I don't copy my lab records from seniors like you." Send.
Then he sat very still on the plastic chair, heart hammering, the TV still going.

qa.a: She said he got 38 in physics again.

qa.q: Why did Binita's post make Yash feel so exposed?
qa.a: It hit his fear that he was not good enough, that he was the dumb one in the batch and everyone knew it, so he felt ashamed and exposed.

qa.a: He could have put the phone down for a few minutes or replied privately to Binita that the joke hurt, rather than answering in public on impulse.

qa.a: She may feel shocked and embarrassed, perhaps defensive, since she may have thought her post was just a light joke.

grounding: In a group chat a teenager is teased about his marks, which touches his fear of not being good enough, and he replies instantly to avoid seeming to agree.

passage:
Dear Vaibhav,

I'm writing this instead of texting because texting is what went wrong on Tuesday.
When you posted in the class group "Rafiq and his 12 out of 40 😆 future engineer", I know you meant it as a joke. But it landed exactly on the thing I lie awake about: that I'm the one in the family who won't make it, the son Abbu will stop bragging about.
I replied in ten seconds. I called you a nerd who has no friends outside class. I didn't think; I just couldn't let the silence sit there, because silence felt like saying "yes, it's true."
I'm not saying sorry yet. I'm saying why.

Rafiq

qa.q: How did Rafiq say his marks were described in the class group?
qa.a: As "Rafiq and his 12 out of 40 😆 future engineer."

qa.q: Why did Rafiq reply so fast?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and afraid of not being good enough, and staying silent felt like admitting the joke was true.

qa.q: What turning point is Rafiq using by writing this letter?
qa.a: He is stepping out of the quick-reply cycle and explaining calmly what hurt, which gives Vaibhav a chance to understand before things escalate.

qa.q: What might Vaibhav be experiencing when he reads the letter?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a bit guilty to learn his joke hit a real fear, and stung by the insult Rafiq sent back.

grounding: A teenager explains how a public joke about his marks hit his fear of not being good enough and why he replied before thinking.

You want the real story, Wasim? Fine. I'm Harsha, I'm sixteen, and I'm not proud of that night.
So the class chat was busy after results, and someone posts, "Harsha topping the list… from the bottom 🥇." Everyone reacts. Like, instantly.
And the thing is, I'd already been thinking it. That maybe I'm just not a studying kind of person. Appa's been quiet all week about my marks. So that message didn't feel like a joke. It felt like someone reading my mind out loud.
My thumb just went. I wrote something really rude back, about his face. Didn't even reread it. Because if I stayed quiet, then everyone would think I agreed.

qa.a: It said "Harsha topping the list… from the bottom 🥇."

qa.q: Why did the message feel like more than a joke to Harsha?
qa.a: It hit a fear Harsha already had, that he was not a studying kind of person, so he felt exposed and ashamed, as if someone read his mind out loud.

qa.q: What turning point was available to Harsha in that moment?
qa.a: He could have waited and reread before replying, or messaged someone he trusts about how it hurt, rather than firing back in public.

qa.q: What might Wasim be experiencing as Harsha tells this story?
qa.a: Wasim is probably listening with concern, perhaps surprised to hear how much the joke hurt and how worried Harsha is about Appa's silence.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how a joke about his marks hit his fear of not being good enough and made him reply rudely before thinking.
